items.title: I asked ChatGPT to create an email client
items.content_html:
I asked ChatGPT:

Can you create an email client that works with Linux Mint Cinnamon?
I would like a self-hosted desktop email client that runs through my web browser.

ChatGPT says:

At first, ChatGPT was very responsive and the bare bones of the application was built up fairly quickly. There followed numerous tweaks to improve the application and it was starting to look like an interesting experiment.

It had a fairly basic offering - I could set up multiple IMAP/SMTP accounts, and view emails. 

At this stage, ChatGPT started to slow things down - the process of fine-tuning the setup was being continually delayed by ChatGPT being extremely stingy in what help it gives before this happens:

Which was another delay of a few hours!

For example, in my previous test of the client, I sent a test email to one of my other email accounts. The email was sent and successfully received at the destination email account. But there was no copy of that sent email filed in the Sent folder - either in the client or the webmail for that email account.

I reported this back to ChatGPT, and it said:

When you're ready, I'll walk you through it one command at a time.

Now this is a problem - every time I'm responding to one command at a time, I'm using my free allowance, before ChatGPT halts the process.

It asks me to:

1. Download the new file.
2. Backup the current data.
3. Stop the currently running application.
4. Move the current installation out of the way.
5. Extract the new file to the same location.
6. Rename the file.

At each stage of the above, I had to confirm I'd done it before proceeding - six questions asked and answered - and again I've run out of the free allowance!

Instead, ChatGPT could have listed what needed to be done, and THEN asked me to confirm, but I suspect that at this stage the process is becoming drawn out, to the extent that I would then 'upgrade' to be able to accomplish the tasks quicker.

This was purely an experiment to see what AI could accomplish, and overall, the result is a functioning - but flawed - local email client.

Will I persevere with it? Only time - and I guess quite a lot of time - will tell!

items.title: Hooroo Fastmail!
items.content_html:
After many years as a Fastmail subscriber, today marks the day that my subscription expires.

Unfortunately, they're now far too expensive for me to justify the cost of renewal. I won't go into specifics about my alternative choice(s), just to say that they're now European based and far cheaper than Fastmail.

I don't recall the exact date that I first took out a Fastmail subscription, but I do recall when, in 2014, Fastmail acquired the fastmail.com domain:

FastMail has moved to fastmail.com, @fastmail.com email addresses now available

I thought - at the time - it would be a good idea to snag my 'firstname@fastmail.com' email address, and, as the availability was on a 'first come, first served' basis, I recall getting out of bed during the night, to log on to my account and claim the email address of choice as soon as they became available.

I was successful in snagging the address, but unfortunately could never really use it!

First of all, there was another person with the same first name as myself, and they must have assumed that they had been allocated this new email address - they had sent a few test emails to the address (which I ignored) and eventually they approached me directly and asked for the address (which I again ignored).

Whether or not it was disappointment on the part of the other person, or because I now had an an easily guessable email address, I started to get constant spam to that address - so much so that I had to whitelist the address to known senders only.

So, I guess that, eventually, that email address will become available should that other person still want it!

items.title: Do you remember?
items.content_html:
♬ Do you remember, the 21st night of September? ♬

I know a song about that! Anyway, to the reason for this post.

I've been trying out alternatives to Google Calendar, preferably EU-Based providers.

My main requirements are for event email reminders to work and to arrive on time, plus the ability to search for very old events.

Google Calendar provides both the above, but what about other providers?

  • Zoho: reminders = pass, searches = fail
  • Proton: reminders = pass, searches = fail
  • Tuta: reminders = pass, searches = fail
  • Mailbox: reminders = pass, searches = fail
  • Infomaniak: reminders = pass, searches = fail
  • Mailo: reminders = fail, searches = pass
  • Nextcloud: reminders = fail, searches = pass

As another experiment, I exported a calendar from Google (that I know works) and imported that calendar into both Zoho Calendar and Mailbox Calendar. Then I exported that calendar out of both of them, and did this comparison:

  • Mailbox exported 69 events.
  • Zoho exported 111 events.
  • Google exported 576 events.

There may be technical reasons for the difference, but the fact remains that only Google Calendars is suitable for my requirements.

In the meantime, I'll continue the search for the Holy Grail!

items.title: What's in a DKIM Record?
items.content_html:
I had recently opened a test Aster Mail email account, which allows for one free own domain to be used. For my test using a spare own domain, I was setting up the usual DNS records (MX, SPF, DMARC), but when it came to the DKIM record I was slightly confused - the length of the record was much shorter than I had been accustomed to using.

The current industry standard is RSA, where a 2048-bit key results in a very long string of nearly 400 characters, and this was the format that I was used to.

This key begins with: 

v=DKIM1; k=rsa;

In contrast, Aster Mail were using the more modern Ed25519 format, which produces a much shorter key of exactly 44 characters, and this was a new one to me - I'd never seen it before.

This key begins with:

v=DKIM1; k=ed25519;

Both of the above keys would be TXT records. Because these keys are static, they're not 'rotatable' - you need to have a new key generated, and publish it alongside the old one to avoid delivery gaps, and eventually remove the outdated record once the new one has propagated.

There are other email providers (for example, mailbox.org and Migadu) that provide the DKIM key in a CNAME format - which allows them to rotate the keys automatically on a regular basis.

items.title: Aster Mail Free
items.content_html:
This is a brief 'heads up' of the relative newcomer to email: Aster Mail

It's a very interesting offering, as they allow the use of one's own domain in this free account.

I won't go into any depth about how to sign up for an account, etc. I'm sure that you're capable of finding out how to do that for yourself!

My Observations

First of all, although Aster - the company - is based in the US, their mail servers and infrastructure are run by Hetzner in Falkenstein, Germany. Here's a better explanation of their set up:

Is Aster Safe If It's Based in the US?

After signing up and testing the free 10 GB account, I was quite impressed by the overall set up and the layout of their UI.

It was also easy to set up one of my own personal domains - the instructions were straightforward and in a matter of minutes it was all set up and working.

As I'm still talking about their free account, there are some limitations:

  1. Only one own domain allowed.
  2. A maximum of five aliases allowed. Once an alias is created, you cannot delete it for a month.
  3. No catchall - you have to rely on the five own domain aliases only.
  4. No IMAP/SMTP - access via webmail and installers for Windows, Linux, and macOS.
  5. No auto-forward rules.
  6. Only two mail filters.

The paid plans include more aliases, more custom domains, catchalls, larger attachments, and unlimited mail filters. IMAP/SMTP is available via their 'Aster Bridge'. 

The main 'selling point' of this free account is the use of one's domain. If you're on the lookout for a free home for your own domain emails, it's certainly worth a try!

Update

Although it was easy to set up my own domain - the instructions were clear and logical - I did encounter a problem with my sent emails not being signed.

I reported this to Aster Mail via their Discord channel, and Lucas Findley (The Founder and CEO of Aster Privacy) took the time to work through the problem with myself, and eventually all was good - my sent emails from my own domain were now being signed.

Kudos to Lucas for going 'above and beyond' to assist me!

items.title: Mailo - Teething Problems?
items.content_html:
My use of Mailo actually started because I was seeking an alternative to my Google Calendar.

A few months ago, I had exported all my calendars/events from Google Calendar to Zoho Calendar.

All seemed well, but I discovered that when I tried to search a calendar for a series of older events from previous years - Zoho reported no results!

Now, I knew for a fact (and did subsequently check to confirm) that these old events were searchable in Google Calendar - I found these events going back to 2019.

I hadn't used Mailo before, so I decided to see how their calendars stacked up against Google.

I imported the same calendar from Google into Mailo, and did the same search for the same event that the Zoho Calendar didn't find.

Result? Success! The Mailo Calendar had listed all the older events.

Initially, I was pleased with Mailo - the calendar appeared to be working, with CalDAV easily set up to my mobile phone. The same with setting up the email and the WebDAV.

Until . . .

I had some upcoming calendar events that I wanted reminders for - I set up both email and notifications. On the first event reminder (an all-day event) I set the reminders to 1 hour before the event (2300 hrs). The day of the event, and switched on my mobile phone, the notification 'pinged' - but no email? The following day, a similar event with similar reminders - got the 'ping', didn't get an email!

But . . .

Surprise, surprise! For this event, I received the email at 1100 hrs on the day - some 12 hours late. Of course, some would say 'your time zone is wrong' but when I first set up the account I corrected the time zone and checked it just now to confirm.

Without that email arriving on time, it seemed that the Mailo Calendar just would not cut it for me.

Another problem occurred with emails. I had 2 legitimate emails rejected by Mailo - the subject: 'Mailo Free's security system has refused a message'.

Maybe the problems with both the calendar reminders and also the rejected emails could be teething problems - I'll wait and see.

But for now, it's back to Google Calendar!

items.title: Zoho Mail Forever Free Plan
items.content_html:
Zoho Mail - 'The Forever Free Plan' - is currently available in the US, EU, and India data centers only. Your IP address determines to which data center you are allocated. For example, if you are in NL, you will be allocated to the Amsterdam data center.

Go to: https://www.zoho.com/workplace/pricing.html

Scroll down towards the end of the page:

Click on the 'Sign Up now' to proceed. If you're in NL, you'll be directed to the zoho.eu sign up web page: 

At this point, you need to choose the 'Business Email' option, to be able to use your own domain. The 'Personal Email' option only offers a zohomail email address.

Complete all required fields, including your 'mobile number' to proceed.

Once all is completed, you're allowed to use only one own domain, but can create up to 5 users (5GB storage per user) for that domain.

As with any new provider, it takes time to become familiar with the UI, set up the domain DNS records, users, etc.

items.title: Create and manage email aliases with MXroute
items.content_html:
MXroute Alias Manager lets you create unique email aliases for every website directly from your browser. Stop giving out your real email address—create a dedicated alias for each service and keep your inbox organized.

This is an extension recently made available for the Chrome browser. It lets you create unique email aliases directly from the browser.

For those of you already familiar with MXroute, and have an account, the extension is basically a shortcut for creating forwarders inside the account.

This is quite easy to set up:

1. Install the 'MXroute Alias Manager' from the Chrome Web Store. 

2. Log into your MXroute Account.

3. Go to Advanced/API Keys. Complete the 'Server' and 'Username' fields, then click on 'Create API Key'.

4. Most important - COPY the API Key, and SAVE it somewhere safe, ready for the next phase of the set up.

5. Go back to the installed browser extension (ensure that you 'pin' the extension for easy access).

6. Go to the extension settings and complete the various tabs:

Credentials Tab - Complete the Server, Username, and API KEY fields. Test the connection, and if all is OK, click on 'Save Credentials'.

Settings Tab - Select the default alias format. Choose between Domain Based, Random, and Manual entry. If you have more than one domain, choose the default domain. Click on 'Save Settings'.

Domains Tab - Here you choose the default forwarding destination for your domain.

Aliases Tab: Lists the aliases created in the extension, in addition to any forwarders that have been created in the Admin account. From here, one can also copy or delete aliases.

The aliases created in the extension will also now be added into the admin account, where one can 'fine tune' the forwarder - change the forwarding email address, reject, discard silently, or delete it.

I've set up the extension for creating manual entries, so I may create easier to remember aliases.

The beauty of using this extension is that you don't need to set up your domain as a 'wildcard', thereby setting it up as a primary target for spammers.

That's it - all set up, tested, and working!

items.title: Atomic Mail - My Thoughts
items.content_html:
I signed up for an Atomic Mail account today, and I thought it may be a good idea to set my thoughts on to my blog.

This first image is the log-on screen:

I've set up my password manager (KeePassXC) for this account. Usually KeePassXC offers to save the login credentials, but it didn't on this occasion - I had to create the entry manually.

After entering my user name (first part of my email address) the password screen appears:

After entering the password, I have enabled two-factor authentication (2FA) so then the 2FA screen appears:

One can choose from either an authenticator code, or a seed phrase to proceed. For myself, I elect to choose the authenticator code, which is generated from my Aegis phone app:

After entering the code, the webmail finally opens:

As you can see, the layout is fairly basic. There is no option to change to a dark theme.

The email view is set as 'conversation view' - I can't see any way to change that.

A good point is that one allowed 10 aliases - a useful addition considering that some providers may only allow a few or none at all. 

The settings options are fairly basic:

There is no option to create filters, although one can manually move emails into different folders. There's no mention of IMAP/SMTP, so I assume that it's not available. I suppose that is comparable to ProtonMail and Tuta - they rely on webmail and dedicated phone apps.

Atomic Mail does have an Android phone app - available on the Google Play Store - but unfortunately I could not get that to work. I suspect that the 2FA is the problem here. I tried to log in using the app - looking identical to the webmail layout, however when I expecting to see a request for the 2FA code that didn't happen - instead it said something like wrong email address or password, and I couldn't proceed.

I suppose I should have tried again, but this time by disabling the 2FA to see it that would work. I may try that again at a later date.

I could log on the webmail account using my phone web browser without problem.

Today was my first time using Atomic Mail - why not try it for yourself?

items.title: Zoho Mail - a cautionary tale, with a happy ending?
items.content_html:
Once upon a time . . . well, around February 2012 (to narrow it down!), I signed up for a Zoho Mail Free account. A short time later, I guess I must have abandoned it and forgot all about it.

Fast forward to the present day, I've had a Zoho paid account for a few months, and I decided to move one of my domains over to this email provider. All proceeded according to plan - domain was verified, DNS records all propagated, and it just remained to create aliases for that domain.

First problem encountered: I created a few new aliases, but when I tried to add another specific alias to my account, I got this warning:

The email address you have entered belongs to a different deployment/region. Please contact support for assistance.

I looked in my password manager (I still have old databases saved) but could not find anywhere that I had used this domain with Zoho. So, I approached Zoho Support and they gave me a 'rough' indication of the username that the alias had been used. I made a guess at the username and got that right, then I was stumped (of course!) by the password - I made a few educated guesses, but not educated enough! So, the next step was the 'forgotten password?' option. Luckily, I still had the recovery address, and so got the new password - and finally got into the account - the account that I had set up in 2012!

Looking into the Admin Console, I saw that I had deleted the domain in question, but hadn't deleted the alias - and THAT was the big mistake on my part!

Second problem encountered: Now, to get rid of the alias. I tried to delete it, but Zoho wanted me to verify myself using 2FA authenticator code!

Hmm, now this IS a problem!

Where would that code be? I must have saved it somewhere!

What phone was I using 13 years ago? I've slept a few times since then, and can't remember. Would the code be in an authenticator app on that phone anyway? That's the million dollar question!

I was, more or less, resigned to the fact that I wouldn't be able to use that alias in my current Zoho account, but gave it one last try. After further experimentation, the problem was the lack of the authenticator code - whatever I tried, I came up against that brick wall.

Delving further into the account settings, I then looked at the 'MFA Mode' and the 'Authenticator app' option. There was the 'secret key'! I copied that key into my phone authenticator app, and finally managed to complete the deletion of that alias!

Going back into my current Zoho account, I then added that alias - success!

The cautionary tale is: Never abandon a Zoho Mail account if you've attached any own domain aliases to it!

The happy ending?

Well, apart from finally solving the alias problem, I now also had full access to that 2012 account - and that account has 40GB of storage (basic plan of 5GB plus 'Add-on allotted' of 35GB) and 25 licences!
 
Plus, even though it's a free account, I am able to access my emails using IMAP/SMTP, via my choice of desktop and phone apps.

Now, I need to figure out a use for that old account!
